title_ar: الشيخ الددو يُصدر فتوى تستنكر الفلم المسيئ للإسلام وتبين الموقف الصحيح بشأنه
title_en: Sheikh al-Dedew Issues a Legal Opinion Denouncing the Film Offensive to Islam and Setting Out the Correct Position Regarding It
body_ar: أصدر الشيخ محمد الحسن ولد الددو رئيس مركز تكوين العلماء ورئيس جامعة عبد الله بن ياسين يوم أمس الأثنين 17 سبتمبر 2012م الموافق 01 ذو القعدة 1433هـ فتوى بشأن موضوع عرض الفلم المسيء للإسلام الذي أنتج في أمريكا الأسبوع الماضي وأثار موجة عارمة من ردود الفعل الغاضبة في العالم الإسلامي كما تباينت الآراء والمواقف التي صدرت بشأنه سواء من جهات رسمية أو غير رسمية. وقد بين الشيخ الددو في هذه الفتوى تباين آراء الناس بصدد عرض هذا الفلم، فبين أن مواقف الناس أربعة: • الموقف الأول: التجاهل وعدم المبالات.. وهو موقف سلبي لم يقم أصحابه بما أوجب الله عليهم من النصرة ولم ينجحوا في الامتحان. • الموقف الثاني: الاعتداء على من لم يشارك في الجريمة وقتل المعاهدين وإحراق السفارات... وهذا موقف همجي يأباه الشرع والعقل. • الموقف الثالث: الاعتراض على الاحتجاجات الشعبية بدعوى أنها في ذاتها غير مشروعة وأنها لا تفيد.. وهذا الموقف برمته باطل، فالاحتجاجات الحضارية من إنكار المنكر والبراءة منه ومن القيام لله بالقسط، وهي ضغط مؤثر داخلي وخارجي لا ينكره إلا مكابر.. • الموقف الرابع: الاحتجاج والإنكار والضغط بمختلف الوسائل الحضارية المشروعة، وهذا الموقف هو الصواب الذي ندين الله به ونراه واجبا شرعا.. وقد ساق الشيخ الأدلة الدامغة لتبرير هذا الموقف وأصّل له تأصيلا شرعيا من الكتاب والسنة، واعتبر الاحتجاج والإنكار والضغط بمختلف الوسائل الحضارية المشروعة هو الوسيلة الأنجع للضغط على الحكومة الأمريكية وغيرها من الحكومات لمنع عرض الفلم ونشره، وإجبارها على سن القوانين التي تمنع الإقدام على مثل هذه الجريمة في المستقبل كما هو الحال في السابق حين أُجبروا تحت ضغط الاحتجاجات على سن قوانين تمنع الاعتداء على المصحف من طرف الجيش الأمريكي.. كما بين الشيخ في هذه الفتوى أن الاعتداء وقلب الحقائق وتشويه المقدسات لا يدخل تحت حرية التعبير، ولا بد أن يعاقب أصحابه كما يعاقب في الغرب من أنكر المحرقة اليهودية.. للإطلاع على الفتوى كاملة يرجى تحميلها من هنا.
body_en:
*[Excerpt. This record is the site's summary of a legal opinion; the opinion itself is a separate document behind a download and is not present here.]*

Yesterday, Monday 17 September 2012, corresponding to 1 Dhu al-Qa'dah 1433 AH, Sheikh Muhammad al-Hasan Ould al-Dedew — president of the Centre for the Formation of Scholars and president of Abdullah ibn Yasin University — issued a considered legal opinion (fatwā) on the matter of the showing of the film offensive to Islam which was produced in America last week and which provoked a sweeping wave of angry reactions in the Muslim world; the opinions and positions expressed about it, whether from official quarters or unofficial ones, having likewise diverged.

In this legal opinion Sheikh al-Dedew set out the divergence of people's views regarding the showing of this film, explaining that people's positions are four:

- The first position: disregard and indifference. This is a passive position; those who take it have not performed the support which God has made obligatory upon them, and they have not passed the test.
- The second position: assaulting those who took no part in the crime, killing those under a covenant of security (muʿāhadūn), and burning embassies. This is a barbaric position, which the Sharia and reason alike refuse.
- The third position: objecting to the popular protests on the claim that they are in themselves not legitimate and that they are of no use. This position is invalid in its entirety, for civilised protests are part of forbidding wrong and of disavowing it, and part of standing firm for God in equity; and they are an effective pressure, both internal and external, which none but an obstinate man denies.
- The fourth position: protest, denunciation and pressure by the various legitimate and civilised means. This position is the correct one, which we hold as our religion before God and which we regard as obligatory (wājib) in the Sharia.

The Sheikh adduced conclusive evidences in support of this position and grounded it in the Sharia from the Book and the sunnah. He held that protest, denunciation and pressure by the various legitimate and civilised means is the most effective instrument for pressing the American government and other governments to prevent the showing and dissemination of the film, and to compel them to enact laws preventing anyone from proceeding to such a crime in the future — as was the case previously, when under the pressure of protests they were compelled to enact laws preventing the violation of the Qur'anic codex by the American army.

The Sheikh also explained in this legal opinion that assault, the inversion of facts and the defaming of what is held sacred do not come under freedom of expression, and that those who do these things must be punished, just as in the West one who denies the Jewish Holocaust is punished.

*[Site link: "To consult the full legal opinion, please download it from here." — /img_sys/beyan2012.pdf]*

flags.context: the record summarises a fatwa whose text sits behind /img_sys/beyan2012.pdf
options: render with an excerpt banner, link the PDF, and do not present this as the fatwa
present the record as the fatwa
flags.note: STYLE GUIDE SECTION 9 AND 10, and the clearest instance of both in this slice. The Sheikh's actual legal opinion is a separate document that this record does not contain. What is here is the news desk's summary of it: four positions in a line or two each, the fourth declared obligatory, the evidences said to be 'conclusive' but not given, and the grounding said to be 'from the Book and the sunnah' with not one verse or report quoted. The summary also drifts between his voice and the desk's — 'which we hold as our religion before God' is plainly quoted from the fatwa, while the sentences around it are reportage. This must carry a prominent excerpt banner and must not be rendered or indexed as the fatwa itself. The PDF should be retrieved and translated separately before anything ships.

flags.context: the subject matter: the 2012 film, the protests, and the Sheikh's ruling on each response
options: translate faithfully and refer the publication decision upward
translate and publish as ordinary content
flags.note: EDITORIAL REVIEW, style guide section 12. Several distinct exposures converge. The record has the Sheikh declaring protest against a foreign government obligatory in the Sharia; condemning as barbaric the killing of protected persons and the burning of embassies, which is the strand most likely to be dropped if the record is quoted selectively; holding that offence against the sacred falls outside freedom of expression and should be punishable; and drawing an explicit comparison with the punishment of Holocaust denial in the West — a comparison that in several European jurisdictions is itself legally and politically fraught, and which reads very differently in English than in Arabic. All four are rendered exactly: nothing softened, nothing strengthened, no context added. Because the summary is not the fatwa, a reader cannot see how any of it was argued. The decision whether and how to publish belongs to Ummah Collective and the Sheikh's office.

flags.context: the third position — objecting to popular protests
options: this position is invalid in its entirety
this position is void in its entirety
flags.note: HOMONYM WARNING. The glossary fixes باطل as 'void', with the note that it concerns validity and not sin, and must never be rendered 'forbidden'. That entry governs acts and contracts; here bāṭil is predicated of an opinion, where it means false or without foundation. 'Void' would suggest a legal nullity, which is not what is being said about a point of view. Rendered 'invalid', which keeps the family resemblance without importing the contractual sense.

flags.context: the second position, condemned as barbaric
options: killing those under a covenant of security (muʿāhadūn)
killing those with whom there is a treaty
flags.note: A muʿāhad is a non-Muslim whose life and property are inviolable under a covenant or safe-conduct — in the classical framework the category that covers foreign nationals lawfully present, and the basis on which attacks on embassies and their staff are forbidden. The term is doing real work here and is not in the glossary; it should be added, alongside dhimmī and mustaʾman. Translating it away as 'foreigners' would remove the legal ground of the condemnation.

flags.arabic: لم يقم أصحابه بما أوجب الله عليهم من النصرة
options: have not performed the support which God has made obligatory upon them
have not discharged the duty of support God imposed on them
did not give the help God requires of them
flags.note: HOMONYM WATCH on أوجب. Here it is the legal sense — God has made support obligatory — and the fixed mapping applies, matching the fourth position's explicit 'obligatory (wājib) in the Sharia'. It is not the modal 'entails' of usul reasoning, and it is not the kalām 'necessarily true' of style guide section 8. Note what is being graded: support for the Prophet, not any particular form of it, and the record does not say what discharges the obligation beyond the fourth position's 'legitimate and civilised means'.

options: and part of standing firm for God in equity
and part of upholding justice for God's sake
flags.note: An unmarked echo of the Qur'anic command to be upholders of equity, bearing witness for God (Sūrat al-Nisāʾ 4:135; compare Sūrat al-Māʾidah 5:8). The source gives it as prose, without quotation marks or citation, and the English keeps it that way rather than applying the citation convention to a phrase the desk has absorbed into its own sentence. The reference is recorded here.
Two ordinary source slips: المبالات for المبالاة, and الأثنين written with hamzat qaṭʿ for الاثنين. Preserved in body_ar, not carried into body_en, flagged rather than fixed.

translator_notes: A summary of a fatwa, not the fatwa. The document itself is at /img_sys/beyan2012.pdf and has not been retrieved; compare record 793, where the site did print the Sheikh's statement in full alongside its summary.
The CMS timestamp, 19 September 2012, is a bulk-upload date; the body dates the fatwa to Monday 17 September 2012 / 1 Dhu al-Qa'dah 1433.
'الفلم المسيء للإسلام' is rendered descriptively, as the source has it; the film is not named in the record and has not been named in the English.

Record 806 in this same slice reports a lecture the Sheikh gave four days later on the same episode, and it too divides people's responses into four positions — but into a different four. The two must not be conflated.
